name: Iatmul
catalog_citation: Staalsen, Philip. 1966. The phonemes of Iatmul. In Frantz, C.I. et al. (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 5, Pacific Linguistics A-7: 69-76. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A7.69 (sealang.net open edition, CC BY-SA 4.0).
catalog_locator: Sec. 5 'Supra-segmental features', 5.1, p. 74 (PDF page 6, rendered and read as image); supporting: sec. 2 vowel inventory p. 69 and 2.1.3 p. 70 (text layer). …
catalog_quote: 5.1. Stress, tone and length are not phonemically pertinent. Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the vowel: /a/ is usually of greater intensity than either /ɨ/ or /ə/, Loudness is not always concurrent with highest pitch of intonation. There is no contrastive stress. 5.2. Pitch becomes important as intonation. The following intonation data is not exhaustive. [p. 74] ... The vowels of Iatmul are /ɨ/, /ə/, and /a/, forming a one dimensional system of high, mid, and low vowel. [p. 69] ... 2.1.3. Low vowel /a/ has allophones: [ʔa] not following a consonant and [a] elsewhere. This phoneme is usually of longer duration than the other vowel phonemes but there is no contrast between [a] and [a:]. [p. 70]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: FILE AND Locator: (8 pp., text layer present; open CC BY-SA 4.0 sealang edition of Pacific Linguistics A-7:69-76). I rendered PDF page 6 = printed p.74 to an image and read it directly. Section '5. SUPRA-SEGMENTAL FEATURES', 5.1 reads exactly: 'Stress, tone and length are not phonemically pertinent. Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the vowel: /a/ is usually of greater intensity than either /ɨ/ or /ə/, Loudness is not always concurrent with highest pitch of intonation. There is no contrastive stress.' followed by '5.2. Pitch becomes important as intonation.' The reported quote matches verbatim; the only difference is punctuation (the original prints a comma, evidently a typo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Staalsen (first-hand, Nyaura dialect at Brugnowi): word stress is non-contrastive and not phonemic; where predictable it follows vowel quality, the full low vowel /a/ carrying more intensity than the high/mid central vowels /ɨ, ə/; no positional (edge-based) rule is stated, and pitch functions only as intonation. The modern grammar (Jendraschek 2012: 91-93, seen only second-hand via Wikipedia) reportedly makes this a ranked weight rule: stress a long vowel, else a closed (CVC) syllable, else the word-initial syllable; diphthongs do not attract stress. Provisional reading therefore weight/quality-sensitive with an initial default (the initial default rests on the unopened Jendraschek 2012).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Staalsen 1966. (Laycock 1965 describes secondary stress only for Wosera Abelam, not Iatmul.)
new_statements.exceptions: Staalsen: 'sometimes'/'usually' hedges only; emphasis intonation (5.2.5) puts tone 3 on the penultimate and a 2-4 glide on the final syllable of short utterances, described as intonation not stress. Jendraschek 2012 (second-hand): in compounds the rules may apply to either the first or the second member.
new_statements.domain_note: Staalsen's statement is about the word/phonemic system generally (isolation forms from elicitation; intonation treated separately at utterance level). Laycock 1965 frames Ndu stress in terms of the 'phonological phrase' (one primary stress per pause-free stretch) but gives no Iatmul-specific rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Staalsen 1966 describes the Nyaura (upriver/western) dialect of Iatmul as spoken at Brugnowi village (his note 2: Laycock calls the Brugnowi dialect Nayura/Nyaura); Laycock 1965's outline is also Nyaura (Yamanambu). Glottolog treats Nyaura as a dialect of iatm1242 (nyau1234 if a dialect code is wanted; language-level key iatm1242 is correct). Jendraschek 2012 (not opened) is based mainly on Korogo (central Iatmul).

sources.quote: 5.1. Stress, tone and length are not phonemically pertinent. Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the vowel: /a/ is usually of greater intensity than either /ɨ/ or /ə/. Loudness is not always concurrent with highest pitch of intonation. There is no contrastive stress. 5.2. Pitch becomes important as intonation.
sources.note: Sec. 5.1 (p.74): stress, tone and length not phonemically pertinent; stress sometimes related to/predictable from vowel quality (/a/ usually more intense than /ɨ/ or /ə/); loudness not always concurrent with intonational pitch peak; 'There is no contrastive stress.' No positional rule given. Sec. 5.2 treats pitch as intonation only.

sources.note: second-hand summary of Jendraschek 2012 pp.91f: words not distinguished by pitch or accent; stress placement rules in descending priority: (1) long vowels are stressed (ti'baadi' [tɨˈmbaːndɨ]), (2) CVC syllables are stressed (ti'kali'ka [tɨˈɡaɾɡa]), (3) otherwise word-initial syllable stressed; in compounds rules may apply to either member; diphthongs are not stressed (p.93).

sources.note: Ch.10 Outline grammar of Iatmul (Nyaura dialect), 10.3 Phonology (pp.113-114) lists phonemes and allophonic differences from Wosera Abelam only; no statement on Iatmul stress. 8.13 (p.101) says phonology in the outline grammars is reduced to a minimum and Wosera distributions are to be assumed unless otherwise stated (Wosera stress, 5.2 pp.29-30: non-phonemic, conditioned by rank of syllable nuclei within the phonological phrase). Implicit at best; not a first-hand Iatmul stress statement.
